ld.description: Even by the lofty standards of Swiss alpinism, the village of Saas-Fee is something else. “Pearl of the Alps” might seem a confusing nickname until you plop yourself in the heart of this gabled, car-free hamlet, from whose perspective the surrounding snow-capped four-thousanders distinctly take on the aspect of an oyster’s lip. Ski resorts around here have embraced intimacy in size and scope — rather than compete with the grandeur of the mountains, they take pride in a humble familiarity with the land. Snow globes rather than glow snobs, if you will. Into this elegant tableau we welcome a relative newcomer: The Capra Saas-Fee.

ld.description: The Swiss Alpine resort of Gstaad is known as the winter destination of choice for the international jet set, and arguably it’s been a little too successful in living up to its reputation — luxury brands are everywhere, and the prevailing vibe is one of extravagant ostentation. Le Grand Bellevue, true to its name, is certainly grand; it’s one of the original Big Four luxury hotels in town, and its century-old exterior is as elegant and finely wrought as ever. But once you’re through its doors, you’ll find a surprise — though unapologetically high-end, Le Grand Bellevue is a luxury hotel of rare tastefulness, and compared to the rest of Gstaad, it’s positively understated.

The hotel offers experiences and activities for every type of weather, from hiking and golfing in summer to skiing and sledging in winter, but the Swiss chalet-style accommodation works all year round. Wood-lined rooms and traditional checked Alpine textiles cocoon guests after hitting the slopes, whilst the floor-to-ceiling window flood rooms with summer sunlight. Of course, spa time is always appreciated, particularly here where the wellness offering includes a pool, sauna, hammam, jacuzzi and more, plus treatments from the likes of cult French beauty brand Biologique Recherche. There’s two restaurants to choose from, plus a cigar lounge and a pop up summer terrace, but gastronomes might enjoy the chance to sit at the Chef’s Table right in the heart of the action.

ld.name: The Chedi Andermatt in Andermatt
ld.description: You wouldn’t know it by looking at the storybook-style mountain scenery, the adorably tiny ski cottages, or the steam trains chugging through the valley, but Andermatt was one Swiss ski resort in need of a facelift. The problem wasn’t aesthetic as much as historical: Andermatt is as pretty as any Alpine village, but it was also occupied by the military for a hundred years, complete with firing range and barracks to house 1,000 soldiers. Change isn’t easy. But sometimes an outsider — in this case, the Egyptian-born developer Samih Sawiris — is the right person to take on the challenge. The result is the sophisticated and ecologically friendly Chedi Andermatt resort, the first European hotel from the Chedi group, a luxury brand that’s well-established in Asia.

ld.name: Villa Principe Leopoldo in Lugano
ld.description: A sparkling glacier-fed lake, candy-colored palaces, breathtaking mountain scenery, a relentlessly highbrow culinary scene — life in Lugano is a pretty easy ride. Maybe even easier? Staying just outside of the city, in a lavish villa that was once the private residence of a prince. Welcome to La Luce Restaurant. You didn’t come to this bucolic corner of Switzerland, after all, to explore bohemian neighborhoods and eat street food — you came to taste the classic pleasures and luxuries of the region. And who knows how to live the good life better than a prince? His one-time home, a stately villa perched high over the lake, has been restored and enhanced to include a first-rate spa suite and a conchiform pool in a lemon grove.

The Grand Hotel Zermatterhof has been here since 1879, and was the favored alpine getaway of the aristocracy, as it is today — though today's visiting aristocrats are as likely to be film stars and rockers as they are royals and statesmen. To get there, you take a funicular from one of the valleys below, or get off the train at the station across the street. Needless to say, you won’t be smelling a lot of tailpipe exhaust — just fresh Alpine air. As for traffic, the only sort you need to look out for will be gliding by on skis or a board. Today, it’s home to a Jack Nicklaus–designed course that’s considered one of Switzerland’s most beautiful, and Guarda Golf Hotel & Residences sits right on its picturesque fairway. This family-owned luxury hotel only opens in summer and winter, an unusual distinction that also makes perfect sense — guests come in season to experience the very best of the place, or to do nothing while enjoying the surrounding scenery, lush and green or snow-covered, as the case may be.

The lakeside setting, at the foot of the Mont Blanc massif, is as magical as ever, while the six rooms and two suites combine sophisticated interior design with classic Alpine materials like fir and Simplon stone. After all, farmers lived in houses on stilts above the waters of this very lake some five thousand years ago — but never quite like this.

It retains an old-world air, from the snow-dusted turrets, wood beams, and coffered ceilings to the billiards room, private ice skating rink, oak-paneled bar, and a richly decorated dining room where even children are required to dress for dinner. Guest rooms are comparatively simple but luxe, with classic wooden furnishings and heavy drapery framing large windows. ld.description: Once a tavern, general store, boarding house, and even a cinema, Falsled Kro has lived many lives since its founding in 1744. Today, it is a peaceful cluster of farm buildings on the South Funen coast, lovingly reimagined as a 26-room inn that helped lay the groundwork for Denmark’s rise in the culinary world. Rooms are all individually styled, some facing the sea, others placed near kitchen gardens. The gourmet restaurant brings together French precision and local Danish produce, while the grounds invite long walks, fireside cocktails, and slow mornings by the coast.

ld.description: Long gone are the days of minimalist sparseness in Scandinavian hotels. In recent years cities like Stockholm have embraced a richly textured and elegant style, and Villa Dagmar, in the city’s upscale Östermalm district, is a fine example: paying tribute to Art Nouveau and other century-old influences, all viewed from a playful contemporary perspective.

ld.name: Stockholm Stadshotell in Stockholm
ld.description: Stockholm is known as one of the capitals of Scandinavian design, so it’s no surprise that Stockholm Stadshotell oozes effortless cool. It took a whole roster of creatives to sensitively revive the hotel’s historic home, a late 19th century Stockholm landmark which originally paid homage to King Oscar I. It’s now a celebration of craftmanship, with minimalist rooms stylishly outfitted by the city’s top designers, from the bespoke burl wood headboards right down to the retro radios. The two restaurants, one housed in the building’s former chapel, shine a light on local ingredients and Nordic flavors with daily changing dishes that come summer, can be enjoyed al fresco in the courtyard. And to suit the Swedish temperatures all year round, there’s also a traditional Scandinavian sauna and cold plunge.

ld.name: Villa Dahlia in Stockholm
ld.description: Created by the Malmström-Cappelen family of Diplomat Collection fame, Villa Dahlia takes its name and spirit from their flower-filled summer cottage. Behind its Brutalist exteriors are soft-toned rooms, Murano glass, and dahlia-red details that brighten the palette. There is art on the walls, the rooftop is made for evening views, pétanque in the courtyard, and a Nordic spa upstairs. Borrow a bike and you will find much of Stockholm within easy reach. Though with so much to enjoy on site, the biggest decision may be whether to venture out at all.

ld.name: Ett Hem in Stockholm
ld.description: In the Sixties Stockholm was the capital of the kind of modernism that’s synonymous with “Scandinavian” design. Nowadays that utopian, vaguely futuristic look is the last thing on anyone’s mind. In the Nordic countries, the best hotels — and their guests — are devoted to something much warmer, a luxe, stylish sort of coziness, and an eclectic approach which makes use of mid-century modernism as just one element among many historical references. And even if Ett Hem’s aesthetic isn’t strictly homegrown — designer Ilse Crawford is London-born, to a Danish mother — the fact is, it’s probably the finest example anywhere of the current tendency in Scandinavian boutique hotel design.

ld.name: Nobis Hotel Stockholm in Stockholm
ld.description: Long before the Swedish design trio Claesson Koivisto Rune reconfigured this 19th-century stone edifice into an eccentric modernist hotel, the site had achieved a certain notoriety; after a spell as a private residence it was home to a bank where, during a 1970s robbery, the term “Stockholm syndrome” was coined. Later it was pressed into service as a high-end apartment complex, and brands like Marimekko and Acne occupied its retail space. It’s in connection with its current incarnation as the Nobis Hotel, however, that we’re moved to take an interest — what’s otherwise a fairly conventional luxury hotel is elevated to something higher, thanks to the contrast of the buildings 19th-century patina and CKR’s contemporary Scandinavian design sensibility.

ld.name: Lydmar Hotel in Stockholm
ld.description: Some of you might remember another Stockholm hotel that went by the Lydmar name, a rowdy, almost painfully hip sort of place, where the focus was very much on the nightlife, and the revelers at times threatened to overwhelm the guests. Well, that was then, and this is now — around the turn of the new millennium that was what boutique hotels were about. Today, more and more, they’re focused on the traditional values of hospitality, and once again the new version of the Lydmar is exemplary.

ld.name: Bank Hotel in Stockholm
ld.description: Bank Hotel’s proprietors are justifiably proud of the 1910 bank building their hotel calls home, but they’re playful enough to name one of their restaurants after a bank robber (Bonnie Parker of Bonnie & Clyde fame). The interiors are a beautifully realized marriage of the building’s classic inheritance and Stockholm’s modern design sense, and though the smallest rooms are small indeed, they’re all impressively luxurious. The city-center location places guests close to many of the capital’s finest arts and culture institutions, as well as no end of restaurants — and the hotel has several of its own, including the Parisian-style Le Hibou, a rooftop bar with an impressive view.

ld.name: Grand Hotel Stockholm in Stockholm
ld.description: With not an ounce of blonde wood and not a single platform bed in sight, the Grand is Stockholm style circa 1874, and the place to stay if you’re a Nobel winner, foreign dignitary, or just an everyday movie star. The location can’t be faulted, in the heart of the city, across from the Royal Palace, with the better rooms looking out over the harbor and the old town. And though it’s been renovated from time to time, to keep up with the demands of modern hospitality, it’s good to see some things never change, like the hotel ballroom, still a meticulous copy of the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

ld.name: Hotel Frantz in Stockholm
ld.description: Stockholm’s Hotel Frantz can authentically claim a long-standing role in Stockholm’s history; the eponymous Frantz was a master tailor for whom this red brick house was built in 1647, which makes it one of the city’s oldest structures. Today it’s a strikingly contemporary and quietly luxurious boutique hotel, making the most of the contrast between its colorful modernist-inspired interiors and its atmospheric historical architecture. The location on the island of Södermalm is central and lively, while the restaurant and bar — including a fairly lavish breakfast spread — make the Frantz a perfectly self-sufficient experience.

ld.name: Arctic Bath in Harads
ld.description: Suspended over a frozen river in the tiny village of Harads, Arctic Bath is unlike anywhere else: an architectural circle of timber enclosing an ice-cold plunge pool, with cabins tucked among the trees and out on the ice. The journey here is part of the adventure, but it is the stillness of the landscape that stays with you. Days are spent snowshoeing, dog sledding, or simply watching the sky shift from rose to gold. The hotel’s sauna ritual and eight-course dinners built around local game and fish round out the sense of deep, elemental immersion.

ld.description: Housed in a 19th-century corner building in Vasastan’s once-quiet Siberia district, Hotel Ruth is a playful, personal project from the Pettersson family. Velvet sofas, custom-made pieces, and rotating art exhibitions sit alongside original tiled stoves and checkerboard floors. Rooms range from compact singles to two spacious suites with Victorian bathtubs. The lobby doubles as a living room, with board games, papers, and a steady hum from the bar. Breakfast is a city favorite, and the mood is friendly, low-key, and full of small surprises.

ld.description: Boutique hotels are just about everywhere now, but it’s still a little bit of a surprise to see Stavanger, Norway represented here. The Eilert Smith Hotel, however, is nothing if not unique. It’s a converted 1930s warehouse by an architect with whom it shares its name, whose early-modernist Functionalist style now stands in stark contrast to the traditional wooden houses and contemporary glass buildings that make up the rest of the cityscape. What makes it such a compelling destination, though, isn’t the building so much as what’s inside: 12 quietly stylish rooms, yes, but most importantly, RE-NAA, one of just two restaurants in all of Norway to be awarded three MICHELIN Stars.

Today Trondheim is much more than a fishing town — it’s Norway’s third-largest city, a university town in a spectacular setting with a booming restaurant scene. And its most glamorous hotel, the Britannia, now hosts style-minded luxury travelers from all around the world.

ld.description: When it comes to hospitality, Norway really does have it all, from avant-garde architectural experiments to this, the oldest family-run hotel in Norway, well into its fourth century in business. Walaker Hotel stands by the side of the Sognefjord, in the village of Solvorn, tucked in dramatically between the mountains and the coast. Its rooms are divided between four distinct buildings, from the main 1930s inn to the oldest one, Tingstova, which dates back to the 1630s.

ld.name: Hotel Union Øye in Norangsfjorden
ld.description: At the end of a fjord and under the jagged peaks of the Sunnmøre Alps, Hotel Union Øye has been welcoming adventurers since 1891. Once the domain of visiting royals, writers, and explorers, the hotel still carries the charm of its original timber structure, shipped in piece by piece, and carefully restored with playful touches like a “ring for champagne” bell (which works!) in the Queen’s Suite. Rooms in the main house evoke Edwardian grandeur, while newer suites in turf-roofed farmhouses are more minimalist and Nordic. Evenings bring piano music, firelit lounges, and a menu that changes with the fjord.

From the outside these glass-and-wood cubes are stunning enough, but it’s from the inside that you begin to appreciate what it is to be a “landscape hotel” — with one or two walls made of full-length glass, each cabin takes in a truly vast forest panorama. (If you’ve seen the film Ex Machina, you’ve seen a partial view of Juvet’s interiors and exteriors.) The Bath House is a spa that frames a cinematic view of a bend in the river, and the restaurant serves a communal dinner made from locally sourced ingredients.

This island in the Steigen Archipelago was once a traders’ outpost, and the hotel’s 1880s-vintage main house is a relic of this era. But the sea cabins, as is evident from the photos, are quite a bit newer. These pared-down larchwood-and-glass structures perch right at the water’s edge, affording vertiginous views through full-length windows from living rooms furnished with mid-century reproduction furniture. Activities include just about anything you can get up to in the Nordic outdoors, which depends heavily on the season, of course — but these cabins are stunning year-round.

Today, many of the cabins are reimagined as guest lodgings, where original timbers sit alongside understated contemporary design. A handful remain unchanged since the 1890s, with no running water, for those who want to experience history in its raw form. Locals still live among them, keeping the village alive. The experience is both immersion and escape, a rare chance to inhabit Lofoten’s fishing past without losing sight of the present.

Countless other details pay homage to the building’s history, from restored tile fireplaces to renovated antique windows and tables built out of 300-year-old pine floorboards. But after a style overhaul by Studio Joanna Laajisto, RUNO’s interior is also a showcase for modern Nordic design.
